name: Deputy
summary: Workforce management for hourly and shift-based teams: rota building, time clocking, timesheet approval and labour-law compliance, with payroll and HR integrations.
best_for: shift-based businesses — hospitality, retail, healthcare, any hourly workforce — that need rostering, clocking and labour-law compliance in one system and have enough staff to clear the minimum spend
skip_if: you run a small salaried desk team: the $30 monthly minimum means you pay for roughly six users whether you have them or not, and salaried staff rarely need shift-level clocking at all
honest_knock: The minimum monthly spend is the number to check before anything else: at $5.50 per user on monthly billing, a team of fewer than about six people still pays the $30 floor, so the headline per-user price is misleading at small scale. Beyond that, the plan you probably want is not the one you first price — auto-scheduling, demand forecasting and labour budgets sit in Core, and SSO, custom access levels and location hierarchies only in Pro, which has no public self-serve checkout. The add-ons stack per user as well, and the payroll add-on is US-only and annual-only.

pricing.notes: (re-read 2026-09-19 on deputy.com/pricing; amounts unchanged since the browser reading of 2026-07-31, which used both billing toggles) Three plans, per user per month and excluding tax. On annual billing Lite is $5, Core $6.50 and Pro $9; switch the toggle to monthly and the same three read $5.50, $7.25 and $10. Add-ons are billed monthly on top. HR is $2 per user, Messaging+ $1.95 per user and Analytics+ $1.50 per user, and the last two are included in Pro. Deputy Payroll enabled by Paycor is $8 per user plus a $49 monthly base fee, available only on annual Core and Pro plans in the US. The page also states a minimum monthly spend of USD $30 / AUD $30 / GBP £20 per invoice on the monthly Lite, Core and Pro plans. Lite and Core start with a free trial; Pro is Contact us rather than self-serve. Two things the page added since: every plan card now carries Deputy AI marked INTRODUCTORY FREE with the line that price and availability may change, so the AI is not a paid-for feature you can hold them to. And a banner across the top offers three months free to businesses that add workforce management and Payroll before 30 November — Payroll being the $8-per-user add-on with the $49 monthly base fee, US-only and annual Core or Pro, so the free months arrive attached to the most expensive thing on the page.

sessions.what: Tested by our team on 24 October 2026 during the Core plan trial, without a card, without sending invitations, publishing a schedule or connecting payroll: Daan created the account and our AI assistant ran the test in Daan's browser. We pasted two made-up team members (with a payroll ID and a base rate) into the bulk importer, exported the team data, and pasted the exported rows back with one changed name.
findings: The bulk importer accepted both rows after we cleared a job title that did not exist yet ('Tester'): only existing job titles are allowed. 'Job Complete: 2 records imported successfully, 0 records failed', and both people showed as Employee, 'Not invited'. The importer's column order differs from the CSV template, so rows copied from the template land in the wrong columns; whether an uploaded file is matched by column name we did not test.
The base rates we pasted in (20 and 25) did not come through: they were empty in the export and no pay rate showed in People.

The team export is prepared in the background ('This can take up to 5 minutes'); ours was ready after about 20 seconds via the notification bell. The CSV had the same 29 columns as the import template, with both people, our payroll IDs and a Deputy ID each. Deputy had filled in a username, a stress profile (24/7) and gender 'Prefer not to say' on its own.

Pasting the exported rows back with their Deputy ID created no duplicates and applied the changed name. But 'Prefer not to say', the gender value from Deputy's own export, was flagged as invalid and had to be cleared first.
After setup, 'Now let's add your team members' had 'Send email invites' ticked by default; we skipped it. The template's sample rows set 'Send Invite' to Y and the role to System Administrator.

The trial bar said '31 days remaining of your Core Plan trial.' and no card was asked. Consent to sales and marketing calls is a line of text under the phone field; SMS marketing is a separate tick box, which we left off.
sessions.note: Findings as written up after the session; no pass/fail per task was scored.

exit_test.what: On 24 October 2026, in the trial account from this test, we exported our two imported test team members through 'Download your existing team member data', then pasted the exported rows back into the importer with their Deputy IDs and one changed preferred name.
exit_test.first_import: Re-importing with the Deputy ID created no duplicates: still 3 of 3 team members, and the changed name came through ('Beta Updated'). But the gender value 'Prefer not to say', which Deputy itself had put in the export, was flagged as invalid in the importer, and we had to clear it before both rows were accepted.
exit_test.awkward: Deputy filled in a username, a stress profile (24/7) and gender 'Prefer not to say' on its own, and that gender value is then rejected on re-import. The export is prepared in the background ('This can take up to 5 minutes'); ours was ready after about 20 seconds via the notification bell.

friction.export_route: People > Add People > Bulk import and update > Update team members > Download; a notification says when it is ready ('can take up to 5 minutes').
friction.format: CSV or XLSX in the import format, including the Deputy ID; no schedules, hours or leave.
friction.reimport: Re-import on Deputy ID works without duplicates, but the gender value from Deputy's own export is rejected, and the base rates were already lost on the first import.
